analysis.one_liner: Made normal trade relations with China permanent, ending the annual review Congress held every year.
analysis.headline: The Senate Finance Committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar in May 2000, but the Senate never voted on it; permanent trade relations with China became law that year through a companion House bill instead.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the law then in force, China's trade status came up every year: Congress could block low-tariff treatment for Chinese goods unless the President waived it, which also gave the United States annual leverage over China's human-rights record. This bill would have ended that routine by letting the President declare normal trade relations with China permanent, once he certified to Congress that China's terms for joining the World Trade Organization matched the deal the U.S. and China struck in November 1999. The change would take effect only when China actually joined the WTO. It is the Senate version of the China trade bill that Congress passed and that became law in 2000.
analysis.who_benefits: US companies that export to China or manufacture there, big retailers and importers that source goods from China, and investors in China's market gain the most: permanent, guaranteed low-tariff access in both directions, with no yearly vote to worry about. American shoppers also benefit over time from cheaper imported goods, and US exporters gain access to a much larger market under the WTO deal terms the bill requires the President to certify.

how_it_helps.text: Lets the President permanently extend normal trade relations (low-tariff treatment) to Chinese products, ending the yearly congressional review under Title IV of the Trade Act of 1974.

Conditions the change on a presidential certification to Congress that China's WTO accession terms are at least as good as the November 15, 1999 US-China agreement, so US companies get the market-opening terms negotiated on their behalf.
Times the change to China's actual WTO accession, so US firms can immediately benefit from China's WTO commitments rather than continue under the annual-waiver system.

analysis.who_pays: Workers in US industries that compete with Chinese imports — manufacturing towns, textile and apparel workers, and others in trade-exposed communities — bear the cost of increased competition with no yearly off-ramp if conditions worsen. The change also removes the annual point of leverage Congress used to press China on human rights, labor rights, and emigration. Consumers who keep their jobs gain from lower prices; the workers and towns on the losing end of import competition do not.

drawbacks.text: Ending the annual review removes the United States' yearly leverage over China on human rights, labor conditions, and emigration — the very mechanism Title IV of the Trade Act of 1974 created, which this bill terminates.

Permanent low-tariff access exposes US import-competing manufacturers and their workers to sustained competition with no regular congressional checkpoint if displacement turns out worse than promised.
The bill's certification requirement is a report by the President, not an approval vote by Congress, so the safeguard it builds in depends entirely on the executive's own judgment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine benefits are real: cheaper goods for consumers and expanded markets for US exporters under China's WTO accession. But the benefits are spread thin across millions of shoppers while the costs concentrate on specific industries and towns, and the bill's safeguard — a presidential report, not a congressional vote — leaves workers with no ongoing check once the annual review is gone. The design tilts toward the interests that asked for certainty of access.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Finance Committee approved it without amendment and it sat on the Senate calendar until the session ended, so it never came to a Senate vote — permanent trade relations with China instead became law that fall through the House-passed companion bill.

narrative.text: Introduced in March 2000 by Senator Roth with 25 cosponsors split 14 Democrats and 11 Republicans.
The Senate Finance Committee ordered it reported favorably without amendment on May 17, 2000, and it was reported to the Senate on May 25.
Placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on May 25, 2000, and never taken up on the floor for the rest of the 106th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US multinationals, retailers, and investors gained permanent access to China's market because the companion House bill became law even though this Senate bill never got a vote. Import-competing manufacturers and the workers in trade-exposed communities are worse off under the permanent arrangement that resulted.

for.name: Sen. William V. Roth Jr.
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and reported it out of the Finance Committee without amendment.

for.name: 14 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Senator Moynihan of New York and Senator Baucus of Montana.

for.name: 11 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Senators Hagel, Gramm, Lugar, and McConnell.

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Made China's permanent normal trade relations a top legislative priority and campaigned extensively for congressional approval of the China WTO trade deal.

against.name: AFL-CIO and major labor unions
against.what_they_did: Ran a large campaign against granting China permanent normal trade relations, arguing it would accelerate manufacturing job losses and remove human-rights leverage.

against.name: A majority of House Democrats
against.role: House minority bloc on the companion bill
against.what_they_did: Provided most of the opposition vote when the House-passed companion bill (H.R. 4444) cleared the House in May 2000.

sides.party_line_note: Support was strongly bipartisan: 25 Senate cosponsors split 14 Democrats and 11 Republicans, the bill cleared the Republican-led Finance Committee without opposition, and both parties' leadership backed the trade deal, with labor unions and most House Democrats leading the opposition.

industries.note: The bill locks in permanent low-tariff access to China's market for US firms and guarantees Chinese goods' access to US consumers, removing the yearly uncertainty that had been the main leverage for conditions on trade. Consumers share the gains through cheaper imports, while import-competing workers bear the losses.

industries.industry: Large retailers and importers of Chinese goods
industries.note: Permanent normal trade relations secures their sourcing of low-cost Chinese products without an annual political risk. Shoppers benefit from lower prices alongside them; the annual human-rights checkpoint disappears with the political risk.

Terminating Title IV removes both the tariff threat and the annual checkpoint these industries and their workers relied on. Their losses fall on the same manufacturing towns and workers the bill offers no ongoing protection to.

China's exporters gain guaranteed, unconditional access to US consumers once it joins the WTO, since the yearly US review of its trade status ends. The human-rights and labor-conditions leverage tied to that review ends with it.
